title: Configuration Management
subtitle: Decoupling immutable artifacts from environment configs, dynamic feature flags, and secret rotation.
keyTakeaways: Build a single immutable container image once (`Build Once, Deploy Anywhere`) and inject environment-specific config at runtime.
Separate **Static Infrastructure Config** (ports, DB URLs) from **Dynamic Runtime Config / Feature Flags** (rate limits, kill-switches, canary percentages).
A bad dynamic configuration push can take down a global fleet in 1 second: always validate schemas and roll out configs progressively just like code.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: In a fleet of hundreds of microservices across multiple regions, hardcoding configuration or rebuilding Docker images per environment violates the Twelve-Factor App principles and guarantees drift between staging and production. Modern configuration management separates concerns into three distinct planes: **Static Boot Config** (injected via Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Environment variables and rolled via immutable pod deployments), **Secrets** (fetched via Vault/AWS Secrets Manager with automatic credential rotation), and **Dynamic Runtime Config** (streamed via long-polling/SSE from a central store like Consul, AWS AppConfig, or LaunchDarkly).
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Build a single immutable container image once (`Build Once, Deploy Anywhere`) and inject environment-specific config at runtime.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Separate **Static Infrastructure Config** (ports, DB URLs) from **Dynamic Runtime Config / Feature Flags** (rate limits, kill-switches, canary percentages).
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Configuration Management:
bullets: **Immutable Config via Container Rollout (GitOps ConfigMaps)**: Provides 100% auditable in git, tested identically to code deployments, rolls out gradually with k8s readiness probes. Best suited for Infrastructure endpoints, connection pool sizing, JVM flags, and environment wiring.

**Dynamic Push Config / Feature Flag Service**: Provides sub-second propagation for emergency kill-switches, dynamic log-level toggling, and a/b canary ramps. Best suited for Feature flags, circuit-breaker/shedding thresholds, and dynamic rate limits.
**Never Store Secrets in Git or Plain ConfigMaps**: Use dynamic short-lived database credentials or envelope encryption via KMS.
**Local Bootstrap Fallback**: Every pod must persist a last-known-good snapshot of dynamic configuration to local disk so a freshly booted pod can start even if the central config service is down.
**Staged Config Rollouts**: Roll out dynamic configuration changes in waves (1% of pods -> 1 AZ -> 1 Region -> Global) with automated metric rollback triggers.
**Avoid Hot-Reloading Connection Pools Unnecessarily**: Keep database topology and thread pool sizing tied to immutable container rollouts where health checks gate each wave.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Configuration Management across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Infrastructure endpoints, connection pool sizing, JVM flags, and environment wiring, suited for environments requiring 100% auditable in Git, tested identically to code deployments, rolls out gradually with K8s readiness probes.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Feature flags, circuit-breaker/shedding thresholds, and dynamic rate limits, where Sub-second propagation for emergency kill-switches, dynamic log-level toggling, and A/B canary ramps.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Many of the largest cloud outages in history (at Google, Meta, Cloudflare, and AWS) were caused not by code deployments, but by a configuration change that bypassed staged rollouts and propagated globally in milliseconds. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Configuration Management introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: takes minutes to roll out across a large fleet; too slow for an emergency 5-second kill-switch.
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: instant global blast radius if a bad rule is pushed without progressive rollout waves.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Configuration Management:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: A bad dynamic configuration push can take down a global fleet in 1 second: always validate schemas and roll out configs progressively just like code.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Emphasize two rules in interviews: **(1) Pods must boot from a Last-Known-Good local cache if the config server is down**, and **(2) Dynamic config changes must use progressive canary rollouts so a typo doesn't brick all regions at once**.
